question: Which forms of separation may ATC apply between aircraft?

options.text: Horizontal only, as vertical separation needs Mode C
Vertical only, as horizontal separation needs radar
Visual, procedural or advisory, depending on the airspace class

explanation: Separation may be vertical, horizontal (longitudinal or lateral) or composite, always to at least a defined minimum.

question: In which airspace classes is separation provided between all flights?

options.text: A only, as only IFR flights are permitted there

explanation: In classes A and B all flights are separated; in class B this includes VFR from VFR.

question: In class E airspace, separation is provided:

options.text: Between VFR flights only, on request from the pilots concerned

explanation: Separation is provided between IFR flights in classes C, D and E; VFR flights in class E are not separated.

question: In which airspace class are IFR flights separated from VFR flights, while VFR flights are not separated from each other?

options.text: Class B, where VFR flights receive traffic information only

explanation: In class C, IFR is separated from IFR and from VFR; VFR receives traffic information about other VFR flights.

question: Special VFR flights are separated:

options.text: From nothing; they rely on see and avoid
From IFR flights, and from each other when prescribed
From IFR flights only when the visibility is below 1500 m in the control zone
Only from other special VFR flights

explanation: Separation is applied between IFR and special VFR flights, and between SVFR flights when prescribed by the appropriate authority.

question: May ATC give a clearance that reduces the spacing between two aircraft below the applicable minimum?

options.text: Yes, if the flights are both receiving a radar service from the same controller

explanation: No clearance shall be given to execute any manoeuvre that would reduce the spacing between two aircraft to less than the applicable separation minimum.

question: When might ATC apply larger separation than the normal minimum?

options.text: Only when an aircraft is flying VFR on top in controlled airspace
For wake turbulence or exceptional circumstances

explanation: Larger separation is applied where wake turbulence requires it or in exceptional circumstances such as unlawful interference.

question: One type of separation is about to be lost. What must the controller do?

options.text: Accept the reduced spacing until the aircraft are well clear of each other
Establish another type of separation first
Ask the pilots to keep a good lookout

explanation: Where one type of separation will be lost, another type must be established before the first is lost.

question: Composite separation combines vertical and lateral separation, each of which may be:

options.text: Not less than the normal minimum, the combination being added for extra safety
Not less than half the normal minimum
Not less than a quarter of the normal minimum
Reduced to zero for a short time

explanation: Composite separation combines vertical and lateral elements, each not less than half the normal minimum, applied by regional air navigation agreement.

question: "Essential traffic" is:

options.text: Controlled traffic not separated from another controlled flight by the minimum
VFR traffic in class G airspace which is close enough to be a collision hazard
Traffic that has declared an emergency

explanation: Essential traffic is controlled traffic to which ATC separation applies but which is not separated by the minimum; essential traffic information is passed to the aircraft.

question: Vertical separation is obtained by assigning different levels expressed in terms of:

options.text: GNSS height above the ellipsoid for aircraft with suitable RNAV equipment
QFE for one aircraft and QNH for the other

explanation: Vertical separation is achieved by requiring aircraft using prescribed altimeter-setting procedures to operate at different levels.

question: Outside RVSM airspace, the vertical separation minimum at or above FL290 is:
explanation: Outside RVSM, the minimum is 1000 ft below FL290 and 2000 ft at or above FL290.

question: In RVSM airspace, which vertical separation applies between FL290 and FL410?

options.text: 1000 ft by day and 2000 ft at night

explanation: In RVSM airspace the minimum is 1000 ft up to and including FL410, and 2000 ft above that.

question: RVSM applies between which flight levels inclusive?

options.text: FL300 and FL500, the levels used by most jet airliners

explanation: RVSM airspace extends from FL290 to FL410 inclusive.

question: For level occupancy purposes, an aircraft is considered at its assigned level when Mode C shows it within:
explanation: The tolerance is ±300 ft of the assigned level, although some States use ±200 ft.

question: May ATC assign a cruising level below the minimum flight altitude established by the State?

options.text: Yes, at any time in radar coverage
Yes, if the pilot accepts responsibility for terrain clearance on the radio

explanation: Cruising levels below the minimum flight altitudes established by the State shall not be assigned, except when specifically authorized.

question: Who determines the lowest usable flight level(s) for a control area?

options.text: The aerodrome control tower nearest to the highest terrain in the area

explanation: The ACC determines the lowest usable flight level(s) for its area and passes it to pilots on request.

question: Within its area, an ACC normally assigns an aircraft:

options.text: One cruising level, except for cruise climb
Any level the pilot wants, without coordination with other units

explanation: The ACC normally assigns only one cruising level within its control area, except when cruise climb is authorized.

question: On ATS routes beyond controlled airspace, where are changes of level normally made?

options.text: At any point, without reference to a navaid or to any reporting point
Over a radio navigation aid, where possible

explanation: Changes of cruising level on ATS routes beyond controlled airspace are normally made over a radio navigation aid where possible.

question: A clearance to change level may specify:

options.text: A time, a place or a rate
Only a waypoint name from the flight plan route

explanation: An aircraft may be cleared to change level at a specified time, place or rate.

question: Aircraft bound for the same destination are assigned cruising levels where practicable:

options.text: In alphabetical order of call signs, to simplify the controller's work
In order of flight plan filing

explanation: Aircraft going to the same destination are, where practicable, assigned levels that suit the approach sequence at the destination.

question: Two aircraft want the same level. One is already at it. Which has priority?

options.text: The aircraft with the earlier estimated time of arrival at the destination
The aircraft already at the level

explanation: An aircraft at a level has priority over others requesting it; where two aircraft are at the same level, the preceding aircraft normally has priority.

question: When may a level vacated by one aircraft be assigned to another?

options.text: Two minutes after the clearance is given
As soon as the first aircraft is cleared to leave it
Once the first aircraft has reported vacating it
When the second aircraft reaches 1000 ft below it and reports it

explanation: A level may be assigned to another aircraft once the previous occupant has reported vacating it.

question: In severe turbulence, when may ATC assign the level being vacated by another aircraft?

options.text: When the other aircraft reports at a level separated by the minimum
When the other aircraft has passed 500 ft from the level, as shown by Mode C
As soon as the other aircraft reports leaving it

explanation: In severe turbulence or cruise climb, the level is not assigned until the other aircraft reports at a level separated by the required minimum.

question: Pilots of two aircraft in direct communication with each other may, with ATC agreement:

options.text: Waive all separation requirements while they remain in visual contact
Keep a specified vertical separation during climb or descent

explanation: Pilots in direct communication may, with their concurrence, be cleared to maintain a specified vertical separation between their aircraft during climb or descent.

question: A pilot may be cleared to climb or descend maintaining own separation in VMC under which conditions?

options.text: Class A, if the other pilot agrees by radio
Classes D and E, by day, below 10 000 ft, on request

explanation: This is permitted in classes D and E, during daylight, below 10 000 ft, on pilot request with the other pilot's agreement, with alternative instructions in case VMC cannot be kept.

question: Lateral separation requires the distance between routes to be at least:

options.text: The navigational inaccuracy plus a buffer
The wingspan of the larger aircraft
Twice the visibility at the flight level, as reported by the pilots

explanation: Lateral separation keeps aircraft on routes whose spacing is not less than the expected navigational inaccuracy plus a safety buffer.

question: Geographical separation is established by:

options.text: A difference of 1000 ft in level, confirmed by Mode C readouts

explanation: Geographical separation is positive indication, by position reports, that aircraft are over different geographical locations.

question: Two aircraft use the same VOR. Lateral separation exists when their tracks diverge by at least:

options.text: 30°, with one aircraft 15 NM or more from the VOR
45°, with one aircraft 15 NM or more from the VOR
10°, with both aircraft 10 NM or more from the VOR
15°, with one aircraft 15 NM or more from the VOR

explanation: From a common navaid: VOR 15°, NDB 30°, dead reckoning 45°, with separation established at 15 NM or more from the aid.

question: Two aircraft use the same NDB. Lateral separation exists when their tracks diverge by at least:

options.text: 30°, with one aircraft 15 NM or more from the NDB
15°, with one aircraft 15 NM or more from the NDB
45°, with one aircraft 30 NM or more from the NDB
20°, with one aircraft 15 NM or more from the NDB

explanation: With an NDB the divergence is 30°; with a VOR 15°; by dead reckoning 45°.

question: Aircraft navigating by dead reckoning are laterally separated when tracks diverge by at least:
explanation: Dead reckoning requires 45° track divergence, with one aircraft at least 15 NM from the point of intersection.

question: Aircraft are using different navaids or RNAV. When is lateral separation established?

options.text: When their protected airspaces do not overlap
When each is at least 10 NM from its own navigation aid and reports it

explanation: When different navaids or RNAV are used, separation exists when the protected airspaces of the routes do not overlap.

question: Parallel RNAV/RNP routes are laterally separated when:

options.text: They are at least 10 NM apart
Their protected airspaces do not overlap
The aircraft fly them at different Mach numbers

explanation: RNAV/RNP parallel routes are spaced so that their protected airspaces do not overlap.

question: Longitudinal separation may be established by:

options.text: Departure time, losing time, time over a point, or holding
Changing the transponder code of one of the aircraft

explanation: Longitudinal separation is in time or distance, and may be established by controlling departure time, losing time en route, time over a point, or holding.

question: The Mach number technique is applied:

options.text: In all airspace classes, whatever the regional agreements
By regional agreement, on same or diverging tracks

explanation: The Mach number technique is used by regional air navigation agreement for aircraft on the same or diverging tracks.

question: For longitudinal separation, two tracks are "same track" when they differ by:

options.text: Less than 30°, measured at the navigation aid or waypoint

explanation: Same track: difference less than 45° or more than 315°.

question: Reciprocal tracks are tracks that differ by:

options.text: More than 45° and less than 135°, or more than 225° and less than 315°

explanation: Reciprocal: more than 135° and less than 225°.

question: Crossing tracks are tracks that differ by:

options.text: Any angle other than exactly 0° or exactly 180°, measured at the crossing point

explanation: Crossing tracks are those differing by 45°–135° or 225°–315°.

question: Two aircraft at the same level on the same track. What basic time separation applies?
explanation: The basic minimum is 15 minutes; it may be 10 minutes where navaids allow frequent determination of position and speed.

question: Same level, same track, departing from the same aerodrome. The preceding aircraft is 20 kt or more faster (TAS). What separation applies?
explanation: 5 minutes applies where aircraft depart from the same aerodrome or report over the same point and the preceding aircraft is at least 20 kt faster.

question: Same level, same track, from the same point. The preceding aircraft is 40 kt or more faster. What separation applies?
explanation: 3 minutes applies when the preceding aircraft is 40 kt or more faster than the following one.

question: Two aircraft at the same level on crossing tracks. What basic time separation applies?
explanation: Crossing tracks at the same level: 15 minutes, or 10 minutes with frequent position and speed checks by navaids.

question: An aircraft climbs through the level of another on the same track. When does 5 minutes' separation apply?

options.text: When the level change starts within 10 minutes of the second aircraft reporting over an exact point
When both aircraft use the same VOR and fly at the same Mach number
Whenever the climbing aircraft is faster

explanation: Basic 15 minutes, 10 minutes with frequent navaid checks, and 5 minutes when the level change is started within 10 minutes of the time the second aircraft reported over an exact reporting point.

question: An aircraft climbs through another's level on a crossing track. What basic separation applies?
explanation: Climbing or descending on crossing tracks: 15 minutes, or 10 minutes with frequent position and speed checks.

question: Two aircraft on reciprocal tracks without lateral separation. When must vertical separation exist?

options.text: From 10 minutes before until 10 minutes after the estimated passing
From 20 minutes before until 20 minutes after, unless both aircraft report passing each other
From 15 minutes before until the aircraft have passed
From 5 minutes before until 5 minutes after the estimated passing

explanation: Vertical separation is provided from 10 minutes before until 10 minutes after the estimated time of passing, unless they are confirmed to have passed.

question: Which condition is required for DME-based longitudinal separation?

options.text: Both aircraft flying at the same Mach number on parallel RNAV routes

explanation: DME separation requires direct controller-pilot communication, with readings taken from on-track DME stations.

question: Same level, same track, both using on-track DME with frequent simultaneous readings. What separation applies?
explanation: 20 NM applies; this may be reduced to 10 NM if the leading aircraft is at least 20 kt faster.

question: Using DME on the same track, the separation may be reduced to 10 NM when:

options.text: The following aircraft is at least 20 kt faster than the one ahead
The leading aircraft is at least 20 kt faster

explanation: 10 NM applies when the leading aircraft maintains a TAS 20 kt or more faster than the succeeding aircraft.

question: When may DME separation for same-track aircraft be applied to aircraft on crossing tracks?

options.text: When both aircraft are in radar contact and on a different frequency from each other
When the track angle is more than 90°
When both report from a DME at the crossing point and the track angle is less than 90°

explanation: The same-track minima apply to crossing tracks if both aircraft report distance from a station located at the crossing point and the angle between tracks is less than 90°.

question: Using DME on the same track, an aircraft climbs through another's level. What separation applies while one aircraft stays level?
explanation: 10 NM applies while one aircraft maintains level flight.

question: Two aircraft on reciprocal tracks are using DME. When may one climb or descend through the other's level?

options.text: When they are 5 NM apart and still approaching each other
When they are 20 NM apart and approaching
Once they have passed and are at least 10 NM apart
At any time, if both are in VMC

explanation: Aircraft on reciprocal tracks may climb or descend through each other's level once they have passed and are at least 10 NM apart.

question: An aircraft flying under the Mach number technique wants to change Mach. What must the pilot do?

options.text: Tell the following aircraft directly on the air-to-air frequency

explanation: The assigned Mach must be kept; approval is requested before changing it, and immediate temporary changes (e.g. turbulence) are reported as soon as possible.

question: Under the Mach number technique, the basic 10-minute separation applies when the preceding aircraft's Mach number is:

options.text: Equal to or higher than the following aircraft's
Within 0.01 of the following aircraft's, whether higher or lower

explanation: 10 minutes applies when the preceding aircraft maintains a Mach number equal to or greater than the following aircraft.

question: Under the Mach number technique, the preceding aircraft is 0.04 Mach faster. What separation applies?
explanation: 0.02 faster gives 9 minutes, 0.03 gives 8, 0.04 gives 7, 0.05 gives 6, and 0.06 gives 5.

question: Under the Mach number technique, the preceding aircraft is 0.06 Mach faster. What separation applies?
explanation: The separation reduces by one minute per 0.01 Mach difference, from 9 minutes at 0.02 to 5 minutes at 0.06.

question: RNAV distance-based separation used instead of 10 minutes with the Mach number technique is:
explanation: 80 NM (150 km) RNAV distance separation may be used with the Mach number technique and direct communication instead of 10 minutes.

question: In RNP 10 airspace, a 50 NM longitudinal minimum requires position reports at least every:
explanation: RNP 20 allows 80 NM with reports at least every 60 minutes; RNP 10 allows 50 NM with reports at least every 30 minutes.

question: In RNP 20 airspace, which longitudinal distance minimum may be used?
explanation: RNP 20 allows 80 NM, with position reports at least every 60 minutes.

question: While the 50 NM minimum is applied, an expected position report is missed. Within what time must the controller act?
explanation: The controller takes action within 3 minutes; if contact is not established within 8 minutes, alternative separation is applied.

question: Within what time of a missed report under the 50 NM minimum must alternative separation be applied if contact is not restored?
explanation: Action is taken within 3 minutes, and alternative separation is applied if communication has not been established within 8 minutes.

question: Separation minima may be reduced when:

options.text: Better navaids, radar or RNAV allow it, after consulting operators
The weather is VMC and the pilots can see each other's lights

explanation: Minima may be reduced with improved navaids, radar, conflict prediction tools or RNAV, after consultation with operators.

question: The basic horizontal radar separation minimum is:
explanation: The basic radar minimum is 5 NM, reducible to 3 NM where radar capability permits.

question: Where radar capability permits, horizontal radar separation may be reduced to:
explanation: The 5 NM basic minimum may be reduced to 3 NM when the radar's capabilities permit.

question: Between aircraft established on the same localizer within 10 NM of the threshold, the reduced radar separation may be:
explanation: 2.5 NM may be applied between succeeding aircraft on the same final approach track within 10 NM of the threshold.

question: In dependent parallel approaches, the minimum radar separation between aircraft on adjacent localizers is:
explanation: 2 NM (diagonal) is applied between aircraft on adjacent localizers in dependent parallel approaches.

question: Wake vortices are most severe behind an aircraft that is:

options.text: Heavy, fast and with gear down
Light and slow, with full flap and gear down for landing
Light, fast and with flaps extended

explanation: Vortices are generated from rotation to touchdown and are strongest behind heavy, slow, clean aircraft.

question: Wake turbulence separation applies to a following aircraft at the same level or:

options.text: Up to 2000 ft below, as vortices sink continuously until they reach the ground
Less than 500 ft above or below

explanation: Vortices spiral and sink, so separation applies to followers at the same level or less than 1000 ft below.

question: For wake turbulence purposes, an aircraft with a maximum take-off mass of 136 000 kg or more is:
explanation: Heavy is MTOM 136 000 kg or more; Medium is less than 136 000 but more than 7000 kg; Light is 7000 kg or less.

question: An aircraft has a maximum take-off mass of 7000 kg. Which wake turbulence category is it?

options.text: Medium, if it has two engines

explanation: Light is 7000 kg or less; Medium is above 7000 kg and below 136 000 kg.

question: Without radar, what wake turbulence separation applies to a medium aircraft landing behind a heavy aircraft?
explanation: For procedural arrivals: medium behind heavy 2 minutes; light behind medium or heavy 3 minutes.

question: Without radar, what wake turbulence separation applies to a light aircraft landing behind a medium aircraft?
explanation: Light behind medium or heavy on arrival: 3 minutes.

question: A medium aircraft departs from the same runway behind a heavy aircraft. What wake turbulence separation applies?
explanation: Light or medium behind heavy, and light behind medium: 2 minutes, for the same runway, parallel runways less than 760 m apart, or crossing paths.

question: A light aircraft takes off from an intermediate part of the runway behind a heavy aircraft that used the full length. What separation applies?
explanation: Taking off from an intermediate part of the runway behind a heavier aircraft using the full length requires 3 minutes.

question: With a displaced landing threshold where flight paths are expected to cross, what wake separation applies?
explanation: 2 minutes applies between light/medium and heavy, or light and medium, when operating on a runway with a displaced threshold where the flight paths are expected to cross.

question: A heavy aircraft makes a low or missed approach. A lighter aircraft takes off in the opposite direction on the same runway. What separation applies?
explanation: Opposite-direction operations where the heavier aircraft makes a low or missed approach and the lighter aircraft takes off or lands in the opposite direction require 2 minutes.

question: When must a heavy aircraft add the word "Heavy" to its call sign?

options.text: On initial contact with an ATS unit
Only when talking to ground control or to an apron management service

explanation: Heavy aircraft include "Heavy" immediately after the call sign in the initial radio contact with ATS units.

question: With radar, what wake turbulence separation applies to a light aircraft behind a heavy aircraft?
explanation: Radar wake minima: heavy behind heavy 4 NM, medium behind heavy 5 NM, light behind heavy 6 NM, light behind medium 5 NM.

question: With radar, what wake turbulence separation applies to a heavy aircraft behind another heavy?
explanation: Heavy behind heavy: 4 NM; medium behind heavy: 5 NM.

question: With radar, what wake turbulence separation applies to a light aircraft behind a medium aircraft?
explanation: Light behind medium: 5 NM; light behind heavy: 6 NM.

question: Why is visual separation used in the vicinity of aerodromes?

options.text: Because radar cannot be used near aerodromes
To replace runway separation at night

explanation: Reduced visual separation in the vicinity of aerodromes allows traffic capacity to be increased.

question: Reduced separation may be applied near an aerodrome when:

options.text: The following aircraft has the preceding one in sight
The aircraft are of the same type and fly at the same speed
The pilots request it, whatever the visibility
The aircraft are on different frequencies

explanation: It may be applied when the aerodrome controller sees each aircraft, when crews keep visual contact with each other, or when the following aircraft reports the preceding one in sight.

question: How is essential local traffic information passed?

options.text: After the aircraft has landed and vacated the runway

explanation: Essential local traffic information is passed without delay to the departing or arriving aircraft concerned.

question: IFR departures are normally separated by:

options.text: Radar vectors issued by the tower controller only

explanation: Departing IFR flights are normally separated by SIDs and standard departure clearances.

question: When may a departing aircraft normally be given take-off clearance?

options.text: When the preceding departure has started its take-off roll
When the preceding departure reports passing 1000 ft and climbing straight ahead
When the preceding departure has crossed the upwind end or turned away
One minute after the previous landing aircraft has touched down

explanation: A departing aircraft is not normally cleared until the preceding departing aircraft has crossed the upwind end of the runway or started a turn.

question: What is the basic time separation between IFR departures?
explanation: Basic spacing between departures is 5 minutes, reduced to 2 minutes (40 kt faster, same track) or 1 minute (tracks diverging by 45° immediately).

question: Two IFR aircraft depart on the same track. The first is 40 kt or more faster. What departure separation applies?
explanation: 2 minutes applies when the preceding aircraft is 40 kt or more faster and both follow the same track.

question: Two IFR departures will follow tracks diverging by at least 45° immediately after take-off. What separation applies?
explanation: 1 minute applies when the tracks diverge by at least 45° immediately after take-off.

question: ATC suggests a take-off direction that is not into wind. Who decides whether to accept it?

options.text: The aerodrome operator, based on the noise abatement rules in force

explanation: A take-off direction not into wind may be suggested for traffic reasons, but the PIC decides whether to accept it or wait for the normal direction.

question: When departures are delayed, ATC normally:

options.text: Clears them in order of size
Clears them in order of estimated departure time and informs operators of delays over 30 minutes
Clears them in the order they ask for start-up, telling operators of any delay over 10 minutes
Clears the airline with the most flights first

explanation: Take-off order is normally by estimated departure time (with deviations allowed), and operators are informed of expected delays exceeding 30 minutes.

question: An IFR aircraft may be cleared for a visual approach when the pilot:

options.text: Has filed a VFR flight plan
Reports that a visual landing is reasonably assured
Can see the runway lights from above the minimum sector altitude and cancels IFR

explanation: A visual approach is possible when the pilot has the terrain in sight with the ceiling at or above the initial approach level, or reports that a visual landing is reasonably assured.

question: During a visual approach, separation from other arriving and departing traffic is provided by:

options.text: The pilot and the operator together, through the flight dispatcher
No one; it is a VFR procedure

explanation: ATC continues to separate an aircraft on a visual approach from other arriving and departing traffic.

question: An arriving aircraft makes a complete instrument approach. Until when may a departure take off in any direction?

options.text: Until the arrival starts its procedure or base turn
Until the arrival is 10 minutes from the runway
Until the arrival passes the final approach fix inbound and starts its descent
Until the arrival reports the runway in sight

explanation: A departure may take off in any direction until the arrival starts its procedure or base turn; then only in a direction at least 45° from the reciprocal of the approach and at least 3 minutes before the arrival is over the runway.

question: An arrival makes a straight-in approach. Until when may a departure take off in any direction?

options.text: Until the arrival starts its descent from the initial approach level
Until 10 minutes before the arrival is over the runway
Until 5 minutes before the arrival is over the runway
Until 3 minutes before the arrival is over the runway

explanation: Any direction until 5 minutes before the arrival is over the runway; then at least 45° from the reciprocal until 3 minutes before (or until a designated fix).

question: When an aircraft is cleared for a straight-in approach, which details need be passed?

options.text: Only the final approach track details
The holding pattern, the sector altitudes and all frequencies
The details of the missed approach only
The full procedure including the procedure turn

explanation: For a straight-in approach, only details of the final approach track need be passed.

question: In segregated parallel operations, the missed approach track must diverge from the departure track by at least:
explanation: The missed approach track of the approach runway must diverge from the departure track of the other runway by at least 30°.

question: In a holding stack, which aircraft normally lands first?

options.text: The aircraft with the least fuel, whatever its position in the stack
The aircraft that arrived first, whatever its level

explanation: Normally the lowest aircraft lands first, and the stack moves down as each level is vacated.

question: Which aircraft is given priority in the landing sequence?

options.text: A hospital aircraft declaring "PAN PAN MEDICAL"
An airliner with connecting passengers that would otherwise miss their flights
A cargo aircraft on a tight schedule

explanation: Priority goes to aircraft compelled to land (MAYDAY/PAN), hospital or medical flights, and aircraft engaged in search and rescue.

question: Aircraft joining a holding stack normally enter at:

options.text: The highest level of the stack
The middle of the stack, to keep the descent rate even

explanation: Stacks are on IAF navaids; aircraft enter at the lowest available level and approaches start from the bottom of the stack.

question: A pilot in a stack wishes to wait for the weather to improve. What may ATC do?

options.text: Keep it at the bottom of the stack
Move the aircraft to another hold or to the top of the stack
Clear it for the approach first, so that it can assess the weather sooner

explanation: An aircraft holding for weather improvement may be cleared to another holding point or to the top of the stack so others can continue.

question: When is an expected approach time (EAT) passed to an aircraft?

options.text: When it enters a holding stack, and it must be acknowledged
When it is 30 minutes from the destination and starting its descent

explanation: The EAT is passed when the aircraft enters a stack and must be acknowledged; "no delay expected" is given when there is no significant delay.

question: An EAT is revised when it changes by:
explanation: A revised EAT is passed when it differs from the previous one by 5 minutes or more.

question: How is time spent holding en route taken into account in the approach sequence?

options.text: The aircraft is moved to the back of the sequence
It is added to the aircraft's EAT, which is then passed to the operator
It is credited to the aircraft

explanation: En-route holding is credited, so the aircraft keeps its due place in the approach sequence.

question: An aircraft is told to hold en route at a point with no published hold. Which pattern should it fly?

options.text: A right-hand pattern unless instructed otherwise
Whichever direction suits the wind at the holding level

explanation: Holding at an unpublished en-route point is a right-hand pattern unless otherwise instructed.
